extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, Administrative Patent Judges (APJs), Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) staff, and litigants/representatives in PTO interference proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for evaluating whether an attorney's creation/use of a manufactured or demonstrative document in an interference/deposition violates PTO disciplinary rules (37 C.F.R. §§10.23, 10.85) and related evidentiary/standing-order requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §10.23(b)(4) — prohibition on dishonesty/fraud/deceit/misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: (b) A practitioner shall not: (4) Engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a ground for professional discipline where attorney conduct involves fabrication or misrepresentation. The Board cites this rule in assessing attorney fitness and conduct; conduct that creates or uses manufactured evidence can fall within this prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §10.23(b)(5) — prohibition on conduct prejudicial to administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: (b) A practitioner shall not: (5) Engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where attorney tactics (e.g., manufacturing exhibits) impede fair, just, speedy, or inexpensive determination of proceedings. The Board finds manufactured evidence that is not timely disclosed can be prejudicial to administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §10.23(b)(6) — prohibition on conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: (b) A practitioner shall not: (6) Engage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad catch-all for conduct undermining professional fitness; creation/use of manufactured evidence may be found to reflect adversely on fitness even if not otherwise covered by specific prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §10.85(a)(4) — knowingly use perjured testimony or false evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) In representation of a client, a practitioner shall not: (4) Knowingly use perjured testimony or false evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements of liability described below. Whether an item is "false evidence" depends on the purpose for which it is used; the rule reaches use of evidence known to be false in the representation of a client.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §10.85(a)(6) — participate in creation/preservation of false evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) In representation of a client, a practitioner shall not: (6) Participate in the creation or preservation of evidence when the practitioner knows or it is obvious that the evidence is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets active participation in producing or preserving false evidence. The Board analyzes whether creation of a demonstrative document constitutes "creation of evidence" and whether the practitioner knew or it was obvious the evidence was false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of liability for 10.85(a)(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements: (1) in representation of a client there is certain evidence; (2) the respondent participated in the creation or preservation of the evidence; and (3) such participation occurred at a time when the respondent knows or it is obvious that the evidence is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three elements must be met and proved by the Director by clear and convincing evidence (see 37 C.F.R. §10.149). The timing and the practitioner's intent/knowledge are critical (e.g., whether the item was contemplated or intended as "evidence" at the time of creation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of liability for 10.85(a)(4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements: (1) in representation of a client there is certain evidence (or testimony); (2) the evidence is false (or testimony is perjured); and (3) respondent used it knowing it was false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director bears burden of proving these elements by clear and convincing evidence. The issue often hinges on whether the item was being used/submitted as evidence and whether the practitioner knew of its falsity when using it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for disciplinary rules (37 C.F.R. §10.149)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director must prove each element of liability by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to allegations under §10.85(a)(4) and (a)(6) (and related disciplinary provisions). The opinion repeatedly emphasizes the need for clear and convincing proof of intent/knowledge and the evidentiary status of the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition(s) of "evidence" — broad vs. narrow constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Evidence" may be broadly defined as any means of establishing a factual matter (something that tends to prove or disprove an alleged fact) or narrowly as matter proffered into a tribunal's record (documents/testimony admitted into evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board examines both definitions (Black's, C.J.S., Wigmore) to decide whether a created demonstrative document qualifies as "evidence" for disciplinary rules. The choice of broad vs narrow construction affects whether creation/use constitutes use of or creation of "evidence" for §10.85.

rubrics_metrics.name: What act/event transforms a document into "evidence" in an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: A document becomes "evidence" when it is presented as an exhibit and (per Standing Order and rules/case law) when it is filed, listed, and relied upon in a motion/opposition/reply or otherwise submitted to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective act(s) — marking as exhibit, presenting/identifying it, filing with the Board in support of a motion, or being relied upon — are necessary to transform a document into "evidence." Mere creation of a document while representing a client, or showing it as a demonstrative without intent to submit, may not make it "evidence." Case law (Lawson v. Enloe, Gunn v. Bosch) and Ryan v. Young are discussed for nuance and conflicting practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing Order and Rule 1.639(b)/Rule 1.671(a) requirements for exhibits and filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing Order: "All evidence (including, transcripts of deposition, documents and things) shall be presented as an exhibit." Rule 1.639(b): proof may be in form of patents, printed publications and affidavits and exhibits identified in affidavits shall be given sequential exhibit numbers; Rule 1.671(a): "evidence consists of affidavits, transcripts of depositions, documents and things."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Standing Order changed prior practice and requires filing/listing of exhibits to be considered evidence in motions/priority phases. The Board interprets these rules to mean exhibits are not "in evidence" unless filed/submitted in accordance with the Standing Order; different APJs have disagreed on whether an exhibit marked/used at deposition automatically becomes evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication requirement to introduce a document as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To introduce a document into evidence it generally must be authenticated by testimony of a witness qualified to identify it or be self-authenticating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of authentication undermines the argument that a document was introduced into evidence at a deposition; the Board noted GX 2195 was not authenticated and therefore had limitations as "evidence" for substantive issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-law principle (Lawson v. Enloe; Gunn v. Bosch) regarding deposition exhibits
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases an exhibit marked for identification and discussed during cross-examination depositions has been deemed part of the record where it was later submitted to the Board and relied upon by a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These cases have been cited to support the proposition that marking and using an exhibit during deposition can make it part of the record; the opinion contrasts that older authority with the Standing Order regime and later decisions (e.g., Lanuza v. Fan, Ryan v. Young) that emphasize filing/listing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ryan v. Young principle on when an exhibit is "in evidence"
rubrics_metrics.description: An exhibit is "in evidence" before the Board only if it is filed (usually in the motions phase), and the exhibit must be listed and discussed in a motion, opposition, or reply; an exhibit is "in evidence" only to the extent it is mentioned and relied upon for a particular motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also: a party may use an exhibit in deposition and later elect not to rely on it; then it is not in evidence. Each motion is to be viewed independently for what evidence is considered. The Board relies on Ryan to hold GX 2195 was only "in evidence" for Chiron's sanctions/suppression motions, not for substantive priority issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and intent matter — a document created before being contemplated as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A document created before a proceeding is initiated or created as an unimplemented plan cannot be "evidence" for purposes of §10.85(a)(4)/(a)(6); some objective act/event must occur for it to be deemed evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board reasons that one cannot "knowingly use" or "create" false evidence if at the time of creation/use the item was not intended or reasonably expected to be used as evidence. The creation of a demonstrative not intended as evidence weighs against finding a disciplinary violation under §10.85.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent/subjective purpose — demonstrative use vs. evidentiary submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a document solely as a demonstrative aid to test witness bias, without intent to submit it as evidence, is distinguishable from creating false evidence for use in the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent's credible testimony that GX 2195 was a demonstrative used to test bias and not intended as evidence was a key factor in the Board's analysis; when counsel would destroy the demonstrative's value by disclosing it, that bears on intent-to-use-as-evidence element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/character of "fabricated evidence" (Black's Law Dictionary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabricated evidence: "false or deceitful evidence that is unlawfully created, usu[ally] after the relevant event, in an attempt to avoid liability or conviction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports view that "fabricated evidence" implies creation with intent to deceive and to serve as evidence; helps distinguish mere demonstratives from fabricated evidence intended for evidentiary use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board's concerns about manufactured evidence and court control
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board stated that creation and use of manufactured evidence and failure to timely admit it detracts from the just, speedy and inexpensive determination of an interference; use of manufactured data without identifying it is "truly extraordinary."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These policy concerns support requiring prior authorization/consultation with the Board before employing such tactics; lack of consultation undermines Board's ability to control the proceeding and increases risk of the item entering the record accidentally or deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of disciplinary vs. adjudicatory responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may find inappropriate conduct in managing an interference, but whether conduct requires a disciplinary investigation or sanction under the Rules is a question for OED (Office of Enrollment and Discipline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the Board finds "inappropriate conduct" and denies suppression, formal discipline (investigation, sanctions under §10.85/§10.23) is handled by OED under applicable procedures. The Board deferred determination of sanctions for later or OED action in the cited case.
